Already
awl-RED-ee
adv.
From all and ready, run together. Webster 1828: before or by this time; at this present time or a specified time. In the New Testament it carries a heavy doctrinal load — the unbeliever condemned already, the mystery of iniquity working already, the harvest white already.

Biblical Definition

Already in the New Testament repeatedly says that a thing supposed to be future is present. Of the unbeliever’s standing: He that believeth on him is not condemned: but he that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God (John 3:18). The condemnation is not a sentence awaiting the last day but a verdict already in force; the judgment day will publish it, not create it. Of evil in the world: For the mystery of iniquity doth already work: only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way (2 Thessalonians 2:7) — written in the first century, of a lawlessness already operating under restraint. Of the harvest: Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest (John 4:35), said in Samaria as the townspeople were coming out to Him. And of Christian attainment, in the great denial that keeps the doctrine of sanctification honest: Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus (Philippians 3:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ALREADY as before or by this time; at this present time or a specified time; noting that the thing spoken of has taken place sooner than might have been expected.

expand to see more

ALREADY, adv. — Before or by this time; at the present time or a time specified.

Noting that a thing has taken place sooner than expected, or before the time in question.

Compounded of all and ready, that is, wholly ready or wholly done.

In Scripture, often used to bring a supposed future condition into the present.

Compare alway, altogether, and other compounds of all in the Authorized Version.

Key Scripture

John 3:18 — "He that believeth on him is not condemned: but he that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God."

2 Thessalonians 2:7 — "For the mystery of iniquity doth already work: only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way."

John 4:35 — "Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest."

Philippians 3:12 — "Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus."

Modern Corruption

John 3:18 says the unbeliever is condemned already, which contradicts the widespread assumption that people are neutral before God until some future assessment, and Philippians 3:12 forbids the opposite error of claiming attained perfection.

expand to see more

The default religious picture has humanity in a neutral condition, waiting for a verdict that will be rendered later on the balance of a life. John 3:18 denies it in the plainest terms: the unbeliever is condemned already, and the stated ground is that he has not believed on the name of the only begotten Son of God. This is the necessary background to John 3:16; a rescue implies present danger. It also explains why the New Testament’s evangelism has urgency in it and modern evangelism often does not. Nobody hurries to warn a man in a neutral condition. Paul’s summary in Ephesians 2:3 is the same doctrine in different words: we were by nature the children of wrath, even as others — by nature, not by verdict pending.

Philippians 3:12 guards the other flank, and it is worth quoting against every perfectionist scheme. Paul — converted on the Damascus road, caught up to the third heaven, author of most of the New Testament epistles — says flatly that he has not already attained and is not already perfect. He describes himself as pressing toward the mark, forgetting the things behind, reaching forth. If Paul at the end of his ministry disclaims perfection, the entire-sanctification and second-blessing traditions are claiming for ordinary believers what the apostle would not claim for himself. And 2 Thessalonians 2:7 completes the picture of the age in which both truths must be held: the mystery of iniquity is already at work, restrained but present, so the believer lives between a condemnation escaped and a perfection not yet reached.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ede (G2235), already, now; krino (G2919), to judge; teleioo (G5048), to complete, to make perfect; Hebrew kebar (H3528), already, long since.

expand to see more

Greek ede (G2235) — already, by this time; condemned already (John 3:18) and white already to harvest (John 4:35).

Greek krino (G2919) — to judge, to condemn; the perfect tense in John 3:18 marks a standing verdict.

Greek teleioo (G5048) — to complete, to bring to the goal; were already perfect (Philippians 3:12).

Greek mysterion (G3466) — a mystery, something once hidden now disclosed; the mystery of iniquity (2 Thessalonians 2:7).

Hebrew kebar (H3528) — already, long ago; a favourite word of Ecclesiastes (Ecclesiastes 1:10).

Usage

"He that believeth not is condemned already (John 3:18) — a verdict in force, not a sentence pending."

"The mystery of iniquity doth already work (2 Thessalonians 2:7) — lawlessness present, and restrained."

"Not as though I had already attained (Philippians 3:12) — the apostle disclaiming what perfectionism claims."
